checks.prompt: A data team wants an assistant that, given a messy CSV and a question, writes analysis code, runs it, reads the traceback when it fails, fixes the code and tries again until it works. A second team wants a document pipeline: extract, then classify, then summarise, always in that order, with the output of each step recorded. Which team's problem is this framework's organizing idea a natural fit for, and why does that fit not extend to the other?
checks.explanation: The unit of composition here is a participant that sends and receives messages, and an application is a conversation between them. That is why the write-code, execute, read-the-error, fix, re-run loop is the framework's signature pattern: it IS a dialogue, and one that a single call cannot close. A fixed extract-classify-summarise pipeline has no dialogue in it — modelling it as one buys flexibility that is not needed while giving up the ordering guarantees a pipeline abstraction provides for free.
options: The first. Its organizing idea is a conversation: participants take turns over a shared message log, and the loop of writing code, having something else execute it and feeding the result back as the next message is precisely a dialogue — which a single model call cannot close. The second team's job is a fixed pipeline with no back-and-forth, so free-form conversation adds flexibility they do not need and cost control they would then have to impose
The second. The framework's strength is fixed ordering of steps with recorded outputs, whereas an iterative fix-and-retry loop requires an explicit state machine that conversation cannot represent
Both equally: the pipeline is simply a conversation in which each participant speaks exactly once, so the same abstraction covers it with no downside
Neither: the framework provides participants but no execution, so the first team must run the code themselves, and the second team's ordering must be enforced outside it

checks.prompt: Summarise this framework's runtime as a moderated group chat. State what an agent minimally is, what the framework's loop does on every turn, how a two-participant conversation differs from one with several, and what happens to the transcript. Then use that model to explain two consequences: why cost grows super-linearly with conversation length, and why a conversation with no explicit stopping rule does not simply end when the work is done.
checks.expected: A correct answer must reduce the framework to its loop: maintain a shared message log, decide who speaks next, call that participant's reply method with the conversation so far, append the reply, and check whether to stop. A participant is minimally a name plus a method that, given the transcript, returns its next message — which may be a model call, a canned reply, the result of executing code, or a tool call. With two participants it is a ping-pong: an opening message starts it and the two alternate. With more, a moderator selects the next speaker each turn — by a fixed rota, by asking a model who should go next, or by a function you supply — and appends their reply to the one shared transcript. The transcript grows monotonically and every participant is handed all of it. The two consequences must follow from that: cost grows faster than linearly because each turn is a model call whose input is the whole accumulated transcript, so turn count and per-turn size both grow, and automatic speaker selection adds a further model call per turn; and the loop has no notion of the work being finished — stopping is a rule you supply, typically a check for a stop token in the message or a cap on turns, so with no rule it continues until a cap trips or tokens are burned. Noting that both should be set — a real stop condition AND a turn or message cap as a backstop — is a plus.

checks.prompt: A team wires up the classic duo for a code task on a server. Their run hangs, producing no output and consuming no tokens. When they fix that, the assistant writes correct code but the loop never ends: the conversation continues until it hits a cap. What are the two causes, and where do they live?
checks.explanation: Two defaults that bite in exactly this order. The participant standing in for the human can be configured to ask a real person never, only when it would otherwise stop, or on every turn — and the classic default is every turn, which is helpful in a notebook and a hang in a server process. Then the stop condition: it typically tests for the model literally emitting a particular token, so if the system prompt never tells the model to emit it, the rule never fires and the conversation runs to whatever cap exists. The corollary is the other half of the same brittleness — if the token appears mid-explanation, the chat ends early.
options: The hang is the human-input setting on the executing participant, whose classic default is to prompt a person on every turn — fine in a notebook, a hang on a server, so it must be set to run autonomously. The non-ending loop is the stopping rule: termination commonly keys on the model literally emitting a stop token, so unless the system prompt instructs it to do so, nothing ever trips the rule

The hang is the missing provider key, which blocks rather than raising, and the loop never ends because the executing participant re-runs the code every turn; both are fixed by capping consecutive automatic replies

The hang is that code execution defaults to a container that must be pulled first, and the loop never ends because the assistant is not permitted to speak last; assigning the final turn to the assistant fixes it
Both are the same cause: the two API generations were mixed, so the stopping rule from one generation is silently ignored by the other's loop

checks.prompt: Implement the conversation runtime. An agent is a dict with `"name"` and `"reply"`, a callable taking the transcript and returning its next message string. A transcript is a list of `{"name", "content"}` dicts. Write `run_chat(agents, opening, select, terminate, max_turns=10)`: start the transcript with `{"name": "user", "content": opening}`, then up to `max_turns` times call `select(agents, transcript)` to choose the speaker, call that agent's `reply` with the transcript, append `{"name": <speaker name>, "content": <reply>}`, and stop early if `terminate(transcript)` is true; return the transcript. Raise `ValueError` if `agents` is empty. Write the selector `round_robin(agents, transcript)`, which picks by how many agent turns have already happened — so the first agent speaks first — cycling round. Write two stopping conditions as callables over the transcript: `TextMention(token)` is true when the LAST message contains the token, and `MaxMessages(limit)` is true when the transcript has reached `limit` messages, counting the opening one. Both must support composition with `|`, producing a condition that is true when EITHER is, and the composed result must itself compose. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The first block is the pattern the whole framework is built around, and it is worth reading as a loop: one participant emits code, the other executes it and puts the real output back into the conversation, and it is that output — not a plan — that makes the next reply say the work is done. Everything after it is about control. Notice that with nothing to trigger the stop rule the cap is the only thing that ends the conversation: the runtime has no idea when the task is finished. Notice too how brittle the usual stop rule is — a participant that merely mentions the token while explaining what it intends to do ends the chat immediately, which is the flip side of a chat that never ends because the model was never told to emit it. The routed example is the other reason to prefer a conversation over a pipeline: the moderator is a function of the transcript, so who speaks next can depend on what was just said. And the watcher makes the cost model visible — every participant is handed the whole growing transcript, every turn.
checks.test:
import contextlib
import io


def agent(name, reply):
    return {"name": name, "reply": reply}


# The pattern the framework exists for: one participant writes code, the other RUNS
# it and reports back, and the result of running it is what drives the next turn.
def brain(transcript):
    last = transcript[-1]["content"]
    if "Task:" in last:
        return "Here is code to run:\n```python\nprint(6 * 7)\n```"
    if "OUTPUT: 42" in last:
        return "The script printed 42. TERMINATE"
    return "Let me reconsider..."


def executor(transcript):
    last = transcript[-1]["content"]
    if "```python" in last:
        snippet = last.split("```python")[1].split("```")[0].strip()
        buffer = io.StringIO()
        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
            exec(snippet, {})
        return f"OUTPUT: {buffer.getvalue().strip()}"
    return "(no code to run)"


assistant, proxy = agent("assistant", brain), agent("proxy", executor)
chat = run_chat([assistant, proxy], "Task: compute 6 * 7 by writing and running Python.",
                round_robin, TextMention("TERMINATE"))
assert [t["name"] for t in chat] == ["user", "assistant", "proxy", "assistant"], chat
assert "OUTPUT: 42" in chat[2]["content"], chat[2]
assert chat[-1]["content"].endswith("TERMINATE"), chat[-1]

# Two participants strictly alternate under a round-robin moderator.
ping = agent("ping", lambda t: "ping")
pong = agent("pong", lambda t: "pong")
chat = run_chat([ping, pong], "start", round_robin, TextMention("never"), max_turns=5)
assert [t["name"] for t in chat] == ["user", "ping", "pong", "ping", "pong", "ping"], chat

# ...and with three, the moderator cycles through all of them.
third = agent("third", lambda t: "third")
chat = run_chat([ping, pong, third], "start", round_robin,
                TextMention("never"), max_turns=4)
assert [t["name"] for t in chat][1:] == ["ping", "pong", "third", "ping"], chat

# A conversation does NOT stop itself: with nothing to trigger the stop rule the
# cap is the only thing that ends it.
assert len(run_chat([ping, pong], "start", round_robin,
                    TextMention("STOP"), max_turns=7)) == 8

# The stop rule is a substring test over the last message, which is exactly why it
# is brittle: a participant merely MENTIONING the token ends the chat early.
chatty = agent("chatty", lambda t: "I will say TERMINATE when I am finished, but "
                                   "first let me explain my plan.")
early = run_chat([chatty], "start", round_robin, TextMention("TERMINATE"), max_turns=9)
assert len(early) == 2, early

# A message-count condition stops on the length of the transcript, opening line
# included, whatever anybody said.
assert len(run_chat([ping], "start", round_robin, MaxMessages(4), max_turns=99)) == 4

# Conditions compose: whichever fires first ends it.
either = TextMention("DONE") | MaxMessages(6)
done_at_three = agent("finisher",
                      lambda t: "DONE" if len(t) >= 3 else "working")
assert len(run_chat([done_at_three], "start", round_robin, either, max_turns=99)) == 4
assert len(run_chat([ping], "start", round_robin, either, max_turns=99)) == 6
assert len(run_chat([ping], "start", round_robin,
                    TextMention("x") | TextMention("ping"), max_turns=99)) == 2

# Who speaks next may depend on WHAT WAS JUST SAID -- the moderator is a function of
# the transcript, not a fixed rota.
def when_code(agents, transcript):
    by_name = {a["name"]: a for a in agents}
    return by_name["reviewer"] if "```" in transcript[-1]["content"] \
        else by_name["writer"]


writer = agent("writer", lambda t: "```python\nx = 1\n```")
reviewer = agent("reviewer", lambda t: "looks fine, DONE")
routed = run_chat([writer, reviewer], "build something", when_code,
                  TextMention("DONE"), max_turns=9)
assert [t["name"] for t in routed] == ["user", "writer", "reviewer"], routed

# Every participant sees the one shared, growing transcript -- which is why cost
# grows with the length of the conversation.
lengths = []
watcher = agent("watcher", lambda t: str(lengths.append(len(t)) or "ok"))
run_chat([watcher], "start", round_robin, MaxMessages(5), max_turns=99)
assert lengths == [1, 2, 3, 4], lengths

try:
    run_chat([], "start", round_robin, MaxMessages(2))
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an empty conversation must be refused")

checks.prompt: A prototype is moved toward production. It runs the model's code with a local executor on the application server, has no turn cap because 'the stop token always works', and was built by copying a tutorial whose imports do not match the installed package. Rank the risk and give the fix for each.
checks.explanation: The ranking matters. Running whatever the model writes on the application host is arbitrary code execution, and the instructions come from text an attacker may be able to influence — a container or sandbox is the baseline. The missing cap is real but bounded: the stop convention is a substring check on a token the model has to be told to emit, so it can both never fire and fire early, which is why you want a stop condition and a cap. And the imports are the version split: two generations of the library share a name in conversation but not an API, so a snippet has to be matched to the release you installed.
options: Executing model-written code locally is the severe one: it is arbitrary code execution driven by text a prompt can influence, so it belongs in a container or sandbox with a reviewed surface. Missing the cap is a cost and liveness risk, because the stop token is a substring convention the model may never emit or may emit early — set a real stop condition AND a turn cap. The imports are a compatibility problem: there are two API generations, whose method names and imports do not transfer, so pin the version and read its own documentation

The import mismatch is the severe one, since nothing runs until it is fixed; local execution is safe because the code is generated rather than user-supplied, and a turn cap is unnecessary once the system prompt reliably instructs the model to emit the stop token
The missing cap is the severe one and the other two are cosmetic: local execution is equivalent to running a container, and the two API generations are interchangeable aliases of the same package
All three are configuration problems solved by the same change — enabling the container executor also pins the API generation and imposes a default turn cap

checks.prompt: Compare this framework against a role-and-task pipeline framework and against a low-level state-graph runtime. For each, say what it is best at and what you give up by choosing it. Then apply the comparison: an engineering team needs an assistant that iteratively writes and runs code against a live dataset, must never exceed a fixed budget per request, and must record a reproducible decision trail for audit. Say what you would recommend and be explicit about the tension in their requirements.
checks.expected: A correct answer must characterise all three. This framework: best at conversational multi-agent work — code-write-and-execute loops, solver-and-critic, debate, and teams where the next speaker depends on what was just said; what you give up is constraint, because free-form dialogue is harder to bound in cost and behaviour, orchestration is implicit in the conversation rather than written down, and there are two API generations to keep straight. The role-and-task framework: best at pipelines describable as specialists working a checklist, in a fixed or manager-delegates order; you give up naturalness for open-ended back-and-forth and emergent dialogue, in exchange for structure. The state-graph runtime: best at explicit control — custom routing, branching, cycles, persistence, resume and human-in-the-loop; you give up convenience, because you wire the nodes, edges and state yourself. The recommendation must engage the tension rather than pick a favourite: the iterative write-run-fix loop is this framework's signature strength, but a hard per-request budget and a reproducible, auditable decision trail are exactly what free-form conversation makes difficult, since the control flow is emergent. Reasonable answers include using the graph runtime so the loop, its retry limit and its state are explicit and inspectable — accepting more wiring for auditability — or using this framework with strict caps, an explicit stop condition and full transcript logging while acknowledging the trail is a conversation rather than a specification. Either is acceptable if the trade is named. A strong answer also notes that running model-written code against a live dataset must be sandboxed regardless of framework, and that cost grows with transcript length so the budget cap has to be enforced by the runtime rather than requested in a prompt.
